unsecured-business-loans|working-capital.h1: Unsecured business loans for working capital
unsecured-business-loans|working-capital.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Working Capital | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|working-capital.desc: How an unsecured term loan can cover a working capital gap for a UK limited company, what lenders check and when another facility may suit better.
unsecured-business-loans|working-capital.lead: A fixed sum with fixed repayments can steady cash flow when the gap is temporary, and suits less well when it keeps coming back.
intro: A working capital gap is the stretch between paying for things and being paid for them. An unsecured term loan covers it with a single lump sum paid into the business account, repaid in equal monthly instalments. There is no asset to value and no legal charge to register, which keeps the process light. The catch is that the loan is a fixed amount, so it works best when you can put a figure on the gap, such as a run of slow-paying customers or a quiet quarter you can see coming.

Lenders look at how cash moves through the business more than at what it owns. Expect them to read several months of bank statements, check that revenue is steady enough to carry the repayments and ask directors for a personal guarantee. For example, a wholesaler with £600,000 in annual revenue that is waiting on a few large invoices might borrow £40,000 over 12 months to bridge the wait. If the gap is permanent rather than temporary, a different kind of facility is often a better match.
uses: Customers paying late
A supplier moves its own customers from 30-day to 60-day terms but still pays staff and suppliers on time. A loan covers the extra month of float.
A planned quiet season
A landscaping firm knows January and February bring little income. It borrows in autumn and repays across the busier months.
Paying suppliers promptly
Settling a key supplier on time can protect a discount or a place in the queue for scarce stock, paid for with the loan rather than the overdraft.
Replacing a withdrawn overdraft
If an overdraft is cut back or withdrawn, a term loan can replace that cushion with a known repayment schedule.
fit: Amounts and terms

Working capital loans tend to be smaller and shorter than expansion loans, often from £5,000 up to a few hundred thousand pounds over six months to three years. A shorter term keeps the total cost down, but each instalment is larger, so check it against your slowest month rather than your average one.
What lenders look for

Bank statements matter most. Lenders want to see consistent income, no regular overdrawn days beyond your limit and no sign that the loan would simply be spent keeping up with existing debts. Filed accounts and a recent list of unpaid customer invoices help show that the gap is temporary.
Repayment against the cash cycle

Instalments are fixed whether the month is busy or not. If your income is lumpy, ask the broker whether any lender offers a longer first period, and set the term so it ends before your next quiet spell begins.
considerations: A fixed sum, not a flexible one

Once borrowed, you pay interest on the whole amount even if the gap closes early. If your need rises and falls from week to week, a revolving credit facility or invoice finance can follow it more closely and may cost less overall.
Covering a gap is not covering a loss

A loan can bridge timing. It cannot fix a business that spends more than it earns. Lenders can usually spot this in the statements, and a broker will tell you if they think the application will struggle.
Personal guarantees
Even with no asset taken as security, directors are normally asked to guarantee a loan personally. Read what the guarantee covers, and for how long, before you sign.
faqs: Is an unsecured loan a good way to cover cash flow?

It can be, when the shortfall is temporary and you can say roughly how long it will last. A fixed loan gives certainty about repayments. If the shortfall keeps coming back or changes in size, a broker may point you towards a revolving facility or invoice finance, which move with your trading.
How much working capital can a company borrow?

Lenders often relate the amount to annual revenue and to how comfortably the business can afford repayments. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above, but the figure for your company depends on its trading history, accounts and bank statements. A broker can give a realistic picture once they have seen them.
What documents will lenders ask for?

Most will want several months of business bank statements, the latest filed accounts and details of the directors. Some also ask for management accounts or a list of unpaid customer invoices to show where the cash is tied up. Having these ready tends to make the process smoother for everyone involved.
Can I use it to pay existing debts?

Some lenders allow it and others do not, and those that do will look hard at why the debts built up. Clearing overdue supplier bills during a temporary squeeze is viewed differently from covering repeated losses. A broker can explain how each lender treats the question.
Will it affect my credit file?

A new loan will appear on the business credit file and often on those of the directors once it is agreed. Lenders usually run credit searches as part of the application. Repaying on time can help the record, while missed payments can harm it. Ask the broker how each lender searches before you apply.

unsecured-business-loans|business-expans.h1: Unsecured business loans for business expansion
unsecured-business-loans|business-expans.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Business Expansion | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|business-expans.desc: How a UK limited company can use an unsecured loan to open a second site, enter a new market or launch a product, and what lenders want to see.
unsecured-business-loans|business-expans.lead: Pay for a second site or a new line without putting property at risk, with instalments you can plan the project around.
intro: Expansion tends to cost more before it earns more. A second site needs a lease deposit, a fit-out and staff before the first customer walks in, and a new product line needs stock and marketing ahead of the first sale. An unsecured loan pays for this without putting property up as security, and the fixed instalments make the project easier to budget. The question lenders ask is whether the growth plan builds on something that already works, so a business with a profitable first site is in a stronger position than one starting from a guess.

Amounts are usually limited by what the company’s existing revenue can support, so unsecured expansion loans tend to sit towards the lower end of the range. For example, a physiotherapy clinic with £450,000 in annual revenue might borrow £60,000 over four years to fit out a second site and recruit two practitioners. Where the plan needs several hundred thousand pounds or more, lenders may want security, and a broker can explain where that line is likely to fall.
uses: A second location
Pay the lease deposit, fit-out and first months of staffing for a branch, clinic, salon or depot while the original site keeps trading.
A new product or service line
Develop, stock and market an addition to what you sell, with the cost spread over the period it takes to build sales.
Entering a new region
Pay for a regional sales hire, a van and a local marketing push to test a market outside your current area.
Taking on a larger customer
Add capacity, whether machine time, staff hours or materials, for a contract bigger than any you have handled before.
fit: Sizing the loan to the plan

Borrow what the plan costs plus a modest margin for overruns, not the largest sum on offer. Expansion budgets usually slip, and a lender will want to see that you have thought about both the costs and the months before income starts.
Matching the term to payback

The term should not run past the useful life of what you are buying, and it should be long enough that instalments do not outrun early revenue. Terms of two to five years are common, and a broker can show how different lengths change the monthly figure.
What lenders check

They look at the existing business: revenue trend, margins, bank statements and how it has handled credit before. A short written plan with realistic projections helps, as does a record of the first site or product doing what you hope the next one will do.
considerations: Early months may be weaker than the plan
New sites and products usually take longer to reach full sales than expected. Make sure the original business could carry the repayments on its own if the new venture is slow to start.
Ceilings on unsecured borrowing
If the project needs more than existing revenue can support, an unsecured lender may offer less than you asked for. A secured loan, or a plan part-paid from your own cash, may be needed.
Personal guarantees on bigger sums

The larger the loan, the more likely lenders are to ask for personal guarantees, sometimes from more than one director. Understand the exposure before you commit to an expansion that stretches the business.
faqs: How much can I borrow to expand my business?

It depends on revenue, profit, trading history and affordability. Unsecured lenders generally lend a proportion of annual turnover, so a larger project may need security or a mix of finance. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above, and a broker can say what suits your plan.
Do I need a business plan?

Not always, but for expansion many lenders like to see one, even a short page. It should cover what you are spending, when it should start earning and how the existing business carries the repayments in the meantime. It helps the broker present your case and shows you have tested the numbers.
Can a newer company borrow to expand?

Loanleaf’s service is for limited companies and LLPs that have traded for at least six months, with annual revenue of £50,000 or more. Beyond that, lenders judge each case on trading record and affordability. Companies with a longer, steadier history generally have more options and can borrow more.
Should I borrow once or in stages?

Staging can reduce risk: a smaller first loan to prove the new site or product, then more once it is earning. The trade-off is time and possibly several applications. A broker can talk through whether one loan or two suits the shape of your plan.
What if the plan costs more than expected?

Ask for a small margin in the original loan and keep some cash back. Increasing a loan midway is not always possible, and a second application will be judged on how the first stage is going. Realistic costings at the start are the best protection.

unsecured-business-loans|buying-equipmen.h1: Unsecured business loans for buying equipment
unsecured-business-loans|buying-equipmen.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Buying Equipment | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|buying-equipmen.desc: When an unsecured loan suits an equipment purchase better than asset finance: used kit, installation costs and mixed purchases for UK limited companies.
unsecured-business-loans|buying-equipmen.lead: Buy used, bespoke or mixed equipment, and pay for installation too, without the machine acting as security.
intro: Equipment is usually financed with asset finance, where the machine itself acts as security. An unsecured loan is the alternative for situations where that route does not fit. A lender may not want to take security over a second-hand lathe bought at auction, a bespoke item with few buyers or a collection of small items such as laptops, tools and furniture. An unsecured loan also lets you pay for everything around the purchase in one go: delivery, installation, training and the first supply of consumables, which an asset finance agreement may not cover.

Because the lender takes no charge over the equipment, you own it from the day you buy it and can sell or replace it without involving them. The price is that lenders rely on the company’s accounts and the directors’ guarantee rather than the asset’s value. For example, a print business buying a £28,000 second-hand press with £4,000 of installation might borrow £32,000 over three years, with the equipment’s working life setting how long the term should be.
uses: Second-hand or auction purchases
Buy a used machine, oven or press from a private seller or at auction, where an asset finance lender may be reluctant to take the item as security.
Installation and set-up
Cover wiring, extraction, groundwork, delivery and commissioning, which can add noticeably to the price of the machine itself.
A mixed bundle of smaller items
Equip a new team with computers, tools, furniture and software under one loan instead of arranging several small agreements.
Bespoke or specialist kit
Pay for equipment built to your own specification, which has few buyers on the open market and so offers little resale value to a lender.
fit: Term against working life

Keep the repayment period shorter than the time you expect the equipment to earn its keep. Three to five years suits much general machinery, while technology that dates quickly may call for a shorter term so you are not still paying for something obsolete.
Amounts

Unsecured equipment loans are generally for smaller to mid-sized purchases. Where the price runs well into six figures, asset finance, with the equipment itself as security, may allow a larger amount at a more comfortable repayment than the company’s revenue alone can support.
What lenders look for

They check the company’s trading and bank statements as for any unsecured loan, and some will ask for the supplier’s quote or invoice. A clear case for how the equipment will earn money, such as extra jobs per week, strengthens the application.
considerations: Asset finance may be better value

Where the equipment is new, standard and holds its value, asset finance can offer lower payments or a longer term because the lender has something to repossess. A broker who handles both can show you the comparison.
VAT and tax treatment
How VAT and tax relief apply to equipment depends on how you buy it and the kind of agreement. Ask your accountant how a loan purchase compares with hire purchase or leasing before choosing.
Paying while the kit is idle
Repayments start soon after the money arrives, even if the equipment is still waiting for delivery or installation. Allow for this overlap in your budget.
faqs: Is an unsecured loan or asset finance better for equipment?

Neither is better in every case. Asset finance uses the equipment as security and often suits new, standard machinery. An unsecured loan suits used, bespoke or mixed purchases and wider costs such as installation. A broker who works with both can explain which suits your situation, and you decide.
Will I own the equipment?

Yes. With an unsecured loan the company buys the equipment outright and the lender has no claim on it, so you can sell or replace it when you wish. With hire purchase you usually own it only after the final payment, and with leasing you generally never do.
Can the loan cover installation and training?

Often, because the loan is not tied to one invoice. Lenders may still ask what the money is for, and some will want to see quotes for the main costs. Give the broker the full picture, including delivery and set-up, so the amount you apply for is right first time.
Do I need to pay a deposit?

Not in the way hire purchase usually asks for one, because the loan is paid to you as a lump sum. If the loan does not cover the full price, you pay the difference from your own cash. Some lenders may pay the supplier directly on larger purchases, which a broker can ask about.
How long does the term usually run?

Terms vary by lender and amount, commonly from one to five years for equipment purchases. A broker will usually suggest a term that does not outlast the equipment’s useful life. A longer term lowers each payment but raises the total cost, so look at both figures before you accept an offer.

unsecured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.h1: Unsecured business loans for buying vehicles
unsecured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Buying Vehicles | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.desc: When an unsecured loan suits a van, car or conversion purchase better than hire purchase, and how UK limited companies should match the term to depreciation.
unsecured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.lead: Buy a used van, pay for the conversion and the extras, and own the vehicle from day one with no finance company’s interest on it.
intro: Business vehicles lose value quickly, which is why most are financed with hire purchase or contract hire. An unsecured loan is an option when those do not fit: buying a used van from a private seller, taking on a vehicle older than a finance company’s age limit, or paying for the costs around the vehicle such as racking, signwriting, a tail lift or a charging point. The loan comes as a lump sum to the company, and the vehicle is registered in your name from the start, with no finance company holding an interest in it.

Lenders look at the company rather than the vehicle, so the age and mileage of the van matter less than the accounts. Expect to be asked for a personal guarantee. For example, a mobile locksmith business borrowing £22,000 over three years for a used van and its racking could repay it in step with the work the van brings in. The term should always end well before the vehicle is worn out or worth very little, which is why shorter terms are sensible for hard-working vehicles.
uses: A used van or car from a private seller
Buy a vehicle that a dealer-backed finance agreement will not cover, often at a lower price than a franchise dealer asks.
Conversion and fit-out
Pay for shelving, a refrigeration unit, a tail lift or a camper-style conversion, which can add thousands to the total cost.
Livery, tracking and the first year’s insurance
Cover the extras that make a vehicle ready to work, such as signwriting, a tracker or insurance paid up front.
Electric vehicle and charging
Put the price of an electric van and a workplace charger under one loan, rather than two separate agreements.
fit: Term against depreciation

Vehicles lose value fastest in their first years. A loan that outlasts the van’s useful life leaves you paying for something worth little. Many businesses choose two to four years, and a broker can show how the monthly figure changes with the term.
Amount and deposit

An unsecured loan is paid to the company, so you control how it is spent and there is no fixed deposit. For a fleet of several vehicles, or high-value ones such as a lorry, hire purchase or a lease may allow a bigger amount for the same revenue.
What lenders check
Company trading history, bank statements and the directors’ credit records. Some ask for the dealer’s invoice. If the vehicle is key to winning work, a short note on what jobs it will carry helps.
considerations: Hire purchase may cost less
Because the vehicle is the security, hire purchase can be cheaper for new or nearly new vehicles. Compare the total repayable under each route, including any final payment or option-to-purchase fee.
Running costs on top
Insurance, road tax, servicing, fuel and parking all come on top of repayments. A van that looks affordable on instalments alone may not be once these are added, so budget the full monthly cost.
Selling or replacing early

With no finance company holding an interest, you can sell the vehicle whenever you like, but the loan stays in place. If you swap the van after two years of a four-year loan you will still be repaying for the old one.
faqs: Can I use an unsecured loan to buy a vehicle?

Yes, if the lender is content with the company’s accounts and the purpose. The money goes to the company, which then buys the vehicle. Some lenders ask for an invoice or quote. A broker can tell you whether an unsecured loan or vehicle finance is likely to suit your case better.
Is it better than hire purchase?

Not necessarily. Hire purchase uses the vehicle as security and can be cheaper for newer vehicles, while an unsecured loan is more flexible about age, seller and extras. The better choice depends on the vehicle and your accounts, and a broker can compare both routes for you.
Does the vehicle’s age matter?

To an unsecured lender, much less than to a vehicle finance company, which often sets age and mileage limits. The lender cares mostly whether the company can afford repayments. A very old vehicle may still be a poor purchase, so think about reliability and the loan term.
Can I buy several vehicles at once?

You can borrow a single amount to buy more than one vehicle, but lenders will look at the total against your revenue. For a larger fleet, a broker may suggest finance secured on the vehicles, which can support a bigger amount. They will explain the options.
Do I need a deposit?

Not in the way hire purchase usually asks for one. The loan is a lump sum, so you decide how it is used. If it does not cover the full cost, you pay the remainder from company cash. Check for arrangement fees as well as the monthly figure when you compare offers.

unsecured-business-loans|buying-stock.h1: Unsecured business loans for buying stock
unsecured-business-loans|buying-stock.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Buying Stock | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|buying-stock.desc: How UK limited companies use an unsecured loan to buy stock for a seasonal peak, a bulk discount or a new range, and how to match the term to sales.
unsecured-business-loans|buying-stock.lead: Place the order before the sales arrive, and size the loan and its term to how quickly your stock sells.
intro: Stock is paid for before it is sold, and the delay between the two is where the pressure builds. A gift retailer buying for Christmas in September, a fashion brand placing a minimum order with an overseas maker or a food wholesaler taking a pallet deal at a discount all pay out first and recover the money as customers buy. An unsecured loan gives the cash to place the order with no need to offer the stock or any property as security. The instalments begin straight away, so the question is whether sales will arrive in time to cover them.

Lenders look at how quickly your stock turns, your margins and your bank statements through previous peaks. For example, an online homeware seller with £800,000 of annual revenue might borrow £50,000 over 12 months to buy for the autumn season, and repay from the sales between October and December. A bulk purchase only makes sense when the supplier’s discount clearly outweighs the interest, and when the goods will sell before they go out of fashion, out of date or out of season.
uses: Seasonal build-up
Buy ahead of a peak such as Christmas, summer or a school term, then repay as sales come in.
A bulk-buy discount
Take a supplier’s price break on a large order, provided the saving is bigger than the cost of the borrowing.
Minimum order quantities
Meet the minimum run a manufacturer or overseas supplier demands, which can be well beyond one month of sales.
Launching a new range
Buy the first batch of a new product line before the first sales show how fast it will move.
fit: Term and the stock cycle

Match the term to how long stock takes to sell, with some room to spare. A 12-month loan suits goods that clear in three to six months, while a six-month loan may suit fast sellers. Instalments that run on long after the goods have sold become a drag on later orders.
Check the margin first

Work out gross margin before you borrow. If stock sells for much more than it cost, the interest is easier to absorb. Thin-margin lines leave little room, and lenders will notice that in the accounts.
What lenders look at

Previous seasons’ bank statements, stock and creditor figures in the accounts, and whether the business has paid suppliers reliably. A purchase order or supplier quote helps show the money is going on stock.
considerations: Unsold stock still has to be paid for

The loan does not shrink if the goods sell slowly. Fashion, perishable and fast-changing technology lines carry the greatest risk, and a discount sale to clear stock can eat the margin that was meant to repay the loan.
A revolving facility may follow the cycle better

If you buy stock repeatedly through the year, a revolving credit facility lets you draw and repay as needed and pay interest only on what you use. A broker may suggest this, or stock finance, where it fits better.
Order deadlines can pass
Seasonal orders have supplier cut-off dates, and an application takes time to arrange. Apply well ahead, and mention the date to the broker at the start.
faqs: Can I borrow to buy stock with an unsecured loan?

Yes. Many lenders will lend to a company for stock if its accounts and bank statements support the repayments. The stock is not taken as security. Some ask for a supplier quote. A broker can tell you whether a loan or a revolving facility looks more suitable for the way you buy.
How long should the term be?

Roughly as long as the stock takes to sell, with a little room for slow sales. For a seasonal build-up that is often between six and twelve months. Longer terms lower monthly payments but raise the total cost, and leave you repaying after the goods have gone.
What if the stock does not sell?

The loan still has to be repaid. Talk to the lender early rather than miss payments. This is why many businesses buy stock in stages rather than all at once, and why a lender will ask about your sell-through history during the application.
Is stock finance different?

Yes. Stock finance, sometimes called inventory finance, uses the stock itself as security and is usually arranged for particular goods, often higher-value items. An unsecured loan is more general. A broker can tell you whether stock finance is available for what you sell.
Will the lender pay my supplier directly?

Normally the money goes to your company’s bank account and you pay the supplier. Some lenders can pay a supplier directly on larger purchases. Ask the broker, particularly if you are buying from overseas and need to arrange payment in another currency.

unsecured-business-loans|hiring-staff.h1: Unsecured business loans for hiring staff
unsecured-business-loans|hiring-staff.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Hiring Staff | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|hiring-staff.desc: How a UK limited company can use an unsecured loan to carry the cost of new hires until they earn their keep, and what lenders ask about the role.
unsecured-business-loans|hiring-staff.lead: Carry the cost of a new hire through the months before they pay for themselves, with repayments you can set against the role.
intro: A new hire costs money for months before it brings in any. Salary, employer National Insurance, pension contributions, a recruitment fee, a laptop and a desk all start in week one, while a salesperson may take half a year to close a first deal and a skilled tradesperson may take weeks to reach full productivity. An unsecured loan can carry the company through that ramp-up, and because the instalments are fixed they are easy to set against the cost of the role. It suits businesses that have work waiting for the extra pair of hands.

Lenders want to see that the hire is a response to demand and not a gamble. They look at gross margin, the order book and the bank statements. For example, a digital agency with £700,000 of annual revenue might borrow £45,000 over three years to hire two designers, covering salaries and recruitment fees until their billable hours reach a profitable level. If the roles are for work that is not yet won, expect more questions about how the repayments are covered if that work is slow to arrive.
uses: Delivery staff for work already won
Take on tradespeople, developers or drivers for confirmed contracts that will pay later than the wages fall due.
A salesperson or account manager
Carry the salary and commission through the months before new customers turn into invoices.
Recruitment and onboarding costs
Pay agency fees, equipment, uniforms, training and certification up front rather than from monthly cash flow.
Moving from part-time to full-time cover
Extend the team’s hours to take on more work or to open for longer, with the cost spread over the term.
fit: Sizing the loan to the ramp-up

Add up the full cost of the role for the months before it covers itself, not the whole year’s salary. A common approach is to borrow enough for six to nine months of cost, then pay from the revenue the hire has brought in.
Term and payback

Terms of two to four years are common. A term that runs far past the point where the hire has paid for themselves means paying interest for no good reason, while one that is too short can load the first months with heavy instalments.
What lenders check
Gross margin and staff costs in the accounts, the bank statements, and the size of the order book or pipeline. Be ready to explain what each new role will deliver, and by when.
considerations: Salaries are fixed, income is not
If the expected work is delayed, the wage bill and the loan instalments both continue. Keep a buffer, and avoid borrowing for several hires at once if the first has not yet proved itself.
Employment costs beyond salary
Employer National Insurance, pension contributions, holiday pay and any benefits add to the cost. Make sure the loan amount reflects the full cost of employment, not just the headline salary.
Not a fix for a wage bill that is already too high
A loan used to keep existing payroll afloat can deepen a problem. A broker may ask what will change in the business to make repayments affordable, and may point to other ways to manage cash flow.
faqs: Can I borrow to pay for new staff?

Yes, many lenders will consider it if the business has the revenue to support the repayments and a clear reason for the hire. The loan goes to the company, which then pays salaries and related costs. A broker can say how lenders may view your case based on your accounts and order book.
How much should I borrow for a hire?

Work out the cost of the role until it is paying its way, including salary, employer National Insurance, pension, recruitment fees and equipment, then add a small buffer. Borrowing a full year’s salary may be more than you need and raises your total repayments. A broker can help test the figures.
Will lenders ask for proof of demand?

Often. They may ask about your order book, signed contracts or pipeline, and look at past revenue growth. They want to see that the extra person will bring in work and not simply add cost. Even a short summary of the work the hire will deliver helps.
What if the new hire does not work out?

The loan still needs to be repaid. This is why a buffer matters, and why some businesses hire in stages or start with a fixed-term contract. Speak to your lender early if repayments become hard, as they may be able to discuss options.
Is the loan interest tax-deductible?

In many cases interest on a business loan is a deductible expense for the company, but the rules depend on your circumstances. Loanleaf cannot give tax advice, so ask your accountant how a loan taken to cover wages would be treated before you decide.

unsecured-business-loans|refurbishing-pr.h1: Unsecured business loans for refurbishing premises
unsecured-business-loans|refurbishing-pr.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Refurbishing Premises | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|refurbishing-pr.desc: How tenants and other UK limited companies can pay for a refit or refurbishment with an unsecured loan, and why lease length matters to lenders.
unsecured-business-loans|refurbishing-pr.lead: Pay for a refit on premises you rent, in stages, with a loan term that sits comfortably inside your lease.
intro: Many businesses that refurbish do not own the building. A restaurant on a ten-year lease, a dental practice in rented offices or a salon on a high street has no property to offer as security, and the work still has to be paid for, usually in stages as the contractor reaches each milestone. An unsecured loan covers that cost without involving the landlord’s property, and the repayments can be spread over the years the refurbished space will be used. The lease is the most important document in the process, because the lender will look at how long you have left on it.

Lenders compare the loan term with the lease: borrowing over five years on a lease that ends in three is hard to justify. They also look at trading figures, since a refurbishment should show up as better takings. For example, a café with £350,000 in annual revenue might borrow £35,000 over four years to replace its kitchen extraction and seating, planning the work for the quietest fortnight of the year. A broker can explain how different lenders view lease length, and whether a lease renewal should come first.
uses: Kitchen, extraction and compliance work
Replace equipment or services that need updating to meet regulations, such as fire safety, ventilation or accessibility requirements.
A new customer-facing look
Redo flooring, lighting, counters and seating in a shop, bar, salon or clinic where appearance helps drive footfall.
Splitting or extending space
Add treatment rooms, a mezzanine or a second workstation area to fit more customers or staff within the same lease.
Back-of-house and workshop upgrades
Improve storage, loading areas or workshop layouts, which cuts wasted time even if customers never see them.
fit: Lease length against loan term

A loan term should sit comfortably within the time left on the lease. If the lease is short, a broker may suggest renewing first or choosing a shorter loan, since lenders see an expiring lease as a risk to the trading that pays the loan.
Paying contractors in stages

Contractors usually want a deposit and stage payments, while a loan arrives as a single lump sum, so you manage the payments yourself. Some lenders may release money in tranches on larger projects, which a broker can ask about.
What lenders check
Quotes from the contractor, the lease, recent accounts and bank statements. A landlord’s written consent to the works, where the lease requires it, shows the project can go ahead without surprises.
considerations: Lost trading during the works
If you must close or reduce capacity, takings fall while repayments begin. Plan the programme around your quietest period and keep some cash back to cover the shortfall.
Improvements stay with the landlord

Fixed fit-out usually becomes part of the building, so you may not recover its value when you leave, and some leases require you to put the premises back as they were. Check your lease terms before committing.
Costs can rise during the work
Hidden problems behind walls and floors are common in older buildings. Ask for a fixed-price quote where possible, and borrow slightly more than the quote to cover surprises.
faqs: Can I borrow to refurbish premises I rent?

Yes. Unsecured loans do not need property as security, so tenants can borrow for fit-out and refurbishment. Lenders will look at your lease length, accounts and bank statements. You may also need your landlord’s consent to the work, which is a matter between you and them.
Does lease length matter?

Yes, a great deal. Lenders prefer a loan term that finishes well before the lease does, because losing the premises would hit the income that pays the loan. If your lease is short, a broker can tell you whether a renewal or a shorter loan may help.
Will the lender want to see contractor quotes?

Often, yes. A written quote shows the cost is realistic and that the money is for the stated purpose. Getting two or three quotes also helps you judge the price. Share them with the broker early so the loan is sized properly the first time.
Can I borrow if I own the building?

Yes, though if you own it you may also have the option of a secured loan against the property, which can allow a larger sum and a longer term. A broker can compare secured and unsecured routes, and you can decide whether the security is worth the risk.
Should I borrow for the whole project?

Not necessarily. Some businesses pay part from cash and borrow the rest, which lowers the total interest and shows lenders you have committed your own money. A broker can help you work out a sensible balance for your situation, and whether lenders would want to see it.

unsecured-business-loans|paying-a-tax-bi.h1: Unsecured business loans for paying a tax bill
unsecured-business-loans|paying-a-tax-bi.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Paying a Tax Bill | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|paying-a-tax-bi.desc: How a short unsecured loan can spread a VAT, corporation tax or PAYE bill for a UK limited company, and what to weigh against late-payment charges.
unsecured-business-loans|paying-a-tax-bi.lead: Settle a VAT, corporation tax or PAYE bill on time and repay it over the months that follow.
intro: Tax bills have fixed dates and they do not move to suit your cash flow. VAT falls due shortly after each quarter ends, corporation tax follows the year end, and PAYE and National Insurance are due every month. A business that has just paid for stock or a new hire can find a large VAT bill arriving the week before payroll. Paying late means interest and possibly penalties from HMRC, so some companies borrow over a short term, spreading the cost across the following months rather than draining the account on the due date.

Lenders concentrate on bank statements and on whether the business is sound apart from the bill. For example, a recruitment firm with a £28,000 VAT bill that falls the week after payroll might borrow it over six months and repay from fee income. Some lenders will pay HMRC directly on your behalf. Whatever the arrangement, the loan only helps when the shortfall is a matter of timing, not a sign that the company cannot afford its tax.
uses: A quarterly VAT bill
Cover a large VAT payment that falls just after a heavy month of purchases or a payroll run.
Corporation tax after a strong year
Settle a bill that is bigger than expected, when the profits have already been reinvested in stock, equipment or staff.
PAYE and National Insurance spikes
Cover higher payments following bonuses, a seasonal intake of staff or a new hire.
A liability found on review
Pay an extra amount that comes to light when accounts are finalised or an enquiry is settled, and repay it over a short term.
fit: Short terms
Tax loans are usually repaid over a few months up to a year or two. A short term keeps the interest cost down, but the instalments need to fit alongside the next tax bill you can already see coming.
Amounts

Tax bills financed this way run from a few thousand pounds up to several hundred thousand for larger companies. Lenders will compare the sum with your revenue, and bigger bills may call for more documents.
What lenders check
Bank statements to show regular trading, the HMRC bill or reference, and your accounts. They want to know the tax is a timing issue, so be ready to explain what changed.
considerations: Weigh the cost against late-payment charges

Compare the total cost of the loan with what HMRC would charge in interest and penalties. In some cases HMRC will agree a payment plan, so ask your accountant whether that is available before you decide.
It does not make the next bill smaller
VAT and corporation tax come round again. Setting money aside each month in a separate account makes the next bill much easier to meet than borrowing each time.
Repeat borrowing is a warning sign
If the company borrows for tax every quarter, lenders may see a business that is not setting money aside. A broker may suggest a different plan, and your accountant can help build a tax reserve.
faqs: Can I borrow money to pay HMRC?

Yes. Some lenders offer loans specifically for tax bills, and general business loans can also be used for this. Terms vary, and some lenders pay HMRC directly. A broker can tell you which lenders are likely to look at your situation and what they will want to see.
Is it better than asking HMRC for more time?

It depends. HMRC may agree a payment plan in some cases, and that can cost less than a loan, though it is a decision for you and your accountant to take. A loan gives certainty and clears the debt in one go, which some businesses prefer.
How long is a tax loan repaid over?

Most run over a few months to a couple of years, depending on the lender and the size of the bill. A shorter term keeps total interest lower. Check the instalments against your cash flow, especially in months when another tax payment falls due.
Do I need to show the HMRC bill?

Usually. Lenders may ask for the VAT return, the corporation tax computation or an HMRC statement to confirm the amount and the due date. Having these to hand when you apply makes it easier for the broker to present your case.
Will a tax loan affect my credit rating?

A loan is recorded on the credit file of the business and may appear on those of its directors. On-time repayment can help the record, while late payment can hurt it. Ask the broker how the lender runs its checks before you apply.

secured-business-loans|business-expansio.h1: Secured business loans for business expansion
secured-business-loans|business-expansio.title: Secured Business Loans for Business Expansion | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|business-expansio.desc: How a UK limited company can borrow larger sums for expansion by securing a loan against property, with notes on valuation, legal work and risk.
secured-business-loans|business-expansio.lead: Larger sums and longer terms for a bigger expansion, backed by property or other assets the company owns.
intro: When an expansion plan needs hundreds of thousands of pounds, the amount can go beyond what trading figures alone will support. A secured loan fills that gap by giving the lender an asset to fall back on, most often commercial property, which can allow larger sums over longer terms than an unsecured loan. The lender usually lends a percentage of the security’s value after any borrowing already secured on it, so the starting point is not revenue but what you own. A company that owns its premises might borrow against them to buy the unit next door, add a production line or acquire a competitor.

For example, a manufacturer with freehold premises worth £2.4m and a £900,000 mortgage already on them might ask to borrow a further £400,000 over ten years against the same building, to pay for an extension. The lender would value the property, check the existing lender’s position and look at the accounts to confirm the repayments are affordable. Because legal work and valuation are involved, allow more time than for an unsecured loan, and tell your broker about any deadline from the start.
uses: Buying or building new premises
Raise a deposit or the full cost of a larger unit, warehouse or site, with the new property often forming part of the security.
Acquiring another business
Part-finance the purchase of a competitor or supplier, alongside your own money and sometimes a seller’s deferred payment.
Extending existing premises
Add floor space, a new production line or a showroom to a building you already own.
A multi-stage expansion programme
Pay for several linked steps, such as new machinery, extra premises and staff, under one longer-term loan.
fit: Amounts and terms

Secured loans for expansion often start in the low six figures and can run to several million pounds, over five to twenty-five years depending on the security and the lender. Longer terms bring smaller instalments but a bigger total cost.
Security and loan to value

Lenders usually lend up to a share of the property’s value, and how much depends on the type of property, its location and any existing charges. A professional valuation sets the figure, not the owner’s estimate.
What lenders check

Accounts, bank statements, a plan for the expansion and the title to the security. They also assess whether the company could afford the repayments from its trading, without relying on selling the property.
considerations: The security is at risk

If repayments are missed, the lender can take action against the asset, including selling it. Do not offer property you could not afford to lose, and take independent legal advice if a director’s home is involved.
Costs arrive before the money does

Valuation, legal fees for both sides and arrangement fees are common. For a loan of this size they can reach several thousand pounds, so ask your broker for the full list and add it to the cost of the project.
Long terms can outlast the plan
A twenty-year loan secured on a building can sit on the company long after the expansion has paid back. Check early repayment charges if you may sell the property or refinance later.
faqs: What can I borrow against for business expansion?

Most often commercial property, whether the premises you trade from or another building the company or its directors own. Some lenders also take a debenture, which gives them a charge over company assets. A broker can say which types of security each lender prefers.
How much can I borrow on a secured loan?

It depends on the value of the security, how much is already borrowed against it and whether the company can afford the repayments. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above. A broker will give a clearer view once they know what is being offered as security.
Can I use my home as security?

Some lenders accept a director’s home as security, but this puts the home at risk if the loan is not repaid. It is a serious step, and independent legal advice is wise. A broker can explain which lenders require it and whether other security would work.
How long does a secured expansion loan take to arrange?

Longer than an unsecured loan, because of the valuation and legal work. A straightforward case may take several weeks and a complex one more. If your plan has a deadline, such as an auction or a completion date, tell the broker at the very start.
Can I borrow in stages?

Some lenders allow a loan to be drawn in stages, such as at completion of different building phases, and charge interest only on what has been drawn. Not all do. If your project runs in phases, ask the broker to look for lenders who offer this.

secured-business-loans|buying-equipment.h1: Secured business loans for buying equipment
secured-business-loans|buying-equipment.title: Secured Business Loans for Buying Equipment | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|buying-equipment.desc: When a UK limited company buying large or specialist equipment might use a secured loan instead of asset finance, and what is put at risk.
secured-business-loans|buying-equipment.lead: For large, specialist or bundled equipment purchases that asset finance alone may not stretch to, a loan secured on property or company assets.
intro: Most equipment is financed with asset finance, where the machine is the security. A secured business loan is a different route: the lender takes a charge over property or over the company’s assets generally, and you borrow a sum that the equipment alone could not support. It tends to come into play for large, specialist or tailor-made purchases, such as a production line, a printing press or imaging equipment, where the resale value is uncertain and installation costs nearly as much as the machinery. Lenders are comfortable with these cases once they have something with an established value behind the loan.

The sums are larger and the terms longer. For example, a food manufacturer buying a £600,000 packaging line, with £120,000 for installation and testing, might borrow £720,000 over eight years secured against its factory, with the instalments timed to the extra output the line creates. The loan can be set against the whole project, not just the invoice. The price is that the property is at risk if the company cannot repay, a risk that asset finance places only on the equipment.
uses: A production line or plant
Buy and install a linked set of machines where the sum is too large or the equipment too specialised for standard asset finance.
Medical, laboratory or imaging equipment
Pay for high-value kit that is expensive to move and has a narrow market of second-hand buyers.
Buying several assets at once
Combine machinery, tooling and fit-out in one secured loan, instead of arranging separate agreements for each.
Upgrading to meet new regulation
Replace plant that no longer meets environmental or safety standards, where the cost is high and the date is fixed.
fit: Amounts and term

Secured loans for equipment projects commonly start in the low six figures and can run into millions, over terms of five to fifteen years. Keep the term within the working life of the equipment, even if the property would support a longer one.
Security options

The lender might take a first or second charge over property, a debenture over the company’s assets, or the equipment itself alongside other security. How much it will lend depends on the combined value, after any existing charges.
What lenders look at

Beyond the usual accounts and statements, they ask for the supplier’s quote, a view of how the equipment will raise revenue and evidence of any contracts it supports. Valuations of both property and equipment may be needed.
considerations: Asset finance may put less at risk

If the equipment is standard and holds its value, asset finance keeps your property out of the picture. Ask the broker to compare, so you know what you are trading off when you offer a building as security.
Equipment ages faster than property
A fifteen-year loan against a building can outlive a machine that lasts eight. Aim for a term that ends before the equipment needs replacing, or you may be repaying and buying again at the same time.
Delays still cost money
Instalments begin when the money is drawn, not when the machine is running. Allow for the months of delivery, commissioning and training in your cash flow.
faqs: Why use a secured loan instead of asset finance?

Usually because the amount is large, the equipment is specialised or the purchase includes costs asset finance does not cover. A secured loan can support all of that against property or company assets. Asset finance often puts only the equipment at risk, so it can suit standard purchases better.
Can the equipment itself be the security?

It can, and some lenders combine a charge over the equipment with additional security such as property. Where the equipment is easy to resell, it may carry more weight. Where it is bespoke, lenders usually look for other assets to support the loan.
Does the loan cover installation?

Often, since a secured loan is not tied to one invoice. Lenders may ask for quotes for the main costs. Include delivery, groundwork, commissioning and training in the amount you request, so you do not have to find the difference from your own cash later.
Will the loan appear against the company’s property?

If the security is property, the lender usually registers a legal charge against it, which appears on the title and at Companies House. This is a standard part of the process and is released when the loan is repaid. Your solicitor will explain what is registered.
How long does it take to set up?

Longer than a basic asset finance deal, because of the valuation and legal work. The timetable depends on the security and the lender. If the equipment has a delivery date or a supplier’s price expiry, tell the broker at the start so they can plan around it.

secured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.h1: Secured business loans for buying vehicles
secured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.title: Secured Business Loans for Buying Vehicles | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.desc: How a UK limited company buying a fleet or specialist vehicles can use a secured loan, and why lenders often want security beyond the vehicles.
secured-business-loans|buying-vehicles.lead: Bring a fleet purchase under one loan, backed by property or company assets as well as the vehicles themselves.
intro: A single van is simple to finance with hire purchase. A fleet is different. A haulage firm replacing six lorries, a coach operator adding vehicles for a new contract or a utilities contractor renewing thirty vans has a large sum to find and a depreciating asset to borrow against. A secured business loan can bring the lot under one facility, backed by property, a debenture or a charge over the fleet, and spread over a longer term than the vehicles’ own value would justify. It also leaves the company with a single lender and a single monthly payment.

Vehicles lose value from the day they are registered, so lenders rarely accept them alone as security for a large sum and often ask for property to sit alongside. For example, a regional haulier buying four tractor units at £95,000 each might borrow £380,000 over five years secured against its yard and depot, with the term set to end before the lorries need replacing. The company would repay one loan rather than four agreements, though its property is then exposed if the repayments fail.
uses: Replacing part of a fleet
Renew older lorries, vans or coaches in a planned cycle, rather than one at a time as each breaks down.
Winning a contract that needs more vehicles
Add a block of vehicles to meet a new route, tender or customer requirement.
Specialist vehicles
Buy gritters, access platforms, refrigerated trailers or other purpose-built vehicles that have a narrower resale market.
Replacing several fleet agreements
Clear a mix of hire purchase and lease agreements with one loan, which can simplify payments and paperwork.
fit: Amounts and terms

Fleet loans of this kind often start in the low six figures. Terms usually follow the economic life of the vehicles, commonly four to seven years for heavy vehicles, and should end before major repair costs set in.
Security and depreciation

Because vehicles depreciate, lenders commonly want additional security, such as property or a debenture, and will count the vehicles at a fraction of cost. The structure varies by lender, and a broker can explain what each is likely to ask for.
What lenders check

A fleet schedule with ages and values, customer contracts that use the vehicles, accounts and bank statements. For commercial vehicles, an operator’s licence in good standing is relevant, and maintenance records show that vehicles are looked after.
considerations: Property at risk for assets that fall in value

Putting property behind vehicles means that if the vehicles are worth less than the debt, the building covers the gap. Consider whether hire purchase on each vehicle, secured only on that vehicle, would put less at risk.
Replacement cycles
A longer loan on a short-lived fleet means paying for vehicles that have already gone. If you replace lorries every five years, borrow on a five-year term, not ten.
Running costs and downtime
Fuel, tyres, insurance, servicing and driver costs sit on top of the loan. A vehicle off the road earns nothing but the instalment is still due, so build in a reserve.
faqs: When is a secured loan better than hire purchase for vehicles?

Often when you are buying several vehicles at once, or when the vehicles are specialist and lenders want more security than they offer. Hire purchase puts only the vehicle at risk and can suit single purchases. A broker who works with both can compare the two for your case.
Can the vehicles themselves be the security?

Yes, a lender can take a charge over the vehicles, often alongside other assets. Because they lose value quickly, many lenders count them at well below purchase price and look for additional security, such as property, for larger sums. A broker can explain what each lender is likely to require.
Can I include used vehicles?

Often, though lenders may apply age limits or value them more cautiously. Some will lend against a mixed fleet of new and used vehicles. Give the broker a list showing age, mileage and condition so they can find a lender whose rules fit.
What happens to the security if I sell a vehicle?

If a vehicle is part of the security, the lender usually needs to agree to the sale and may require part of the loan to be repaid or the proceeds to go towards it. Check these conditions before you agree to the loan, especially if you replace vehicles regularly.
Do I still need a personal guarantee?

Possibly. Some lenders ask directors to guarantee the loan as well as taking security over assets. A broker can explain what each lender is likely to require before you apply, so there are no surprises at the offer stage. Ask before you share any documents or sign anything.

secured-business-loans|refurbishing-prem.h1: Secured business loans for refurbishing premises
secured-business-loans|refurbishing-prem.title: Secured Business Loans for Refurbishing Premises | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|refurbishing-prem.desc: How a UK limited company that owns its premises can borrow against them to pay for major refurbishment, with notes on valuation, consents and staged work.
secured-business-loans|refurbishing-prem.lead: Borrow against a building the company owns to pay for major works, over a term that matches the life of the improvements.
intro: A company that owns its premises has an asset that can carry a loan for the work done on it. A secured business loan lets you borrow against the building to pay for a major refurbishment, such as re-roofing a workshop, converting a warehouse floor into offices or remodelling a restaurant and its kitchen. The amounts are usually larger than an unsecured lender would offer, and the repayments run over a longer period, which suits work that will improve the building for decades. Because the work is on the property itself, the lender has a direct interest in how the money is spent.

For example, a family-owned garage group with a freehold worth £1.8m and a £600,000 mortgage might borrow £250,000 over fifteen years to rebuild its showroom and service bay. The lender would value the property, check the existing mortgage and look at plans, quotes and permissions before agreeing. Structural work often needs planning permission or building regulations approval, and lenders will usually want to see these in place before the money is released, so allow time before the builders start.
uses: Structural and roofing work
Repair or replace a roof, floor, cladding or services that the building needs to keep trading safely.
A full remodel or conversion
Re-plan the layout, convert space to a new use or add a floor, where the work needs permissions and a phased build.
Energy efficiency upgrades
Install insulation, heating or solar panels that cut running costs and make the building more attractive to future occupiers.
Bringing a newly bought building up to standard
Pay for the works needed on a property you have just acquired, alongside the purchase finance.
fit: Borrowing against current value

Lenders usually base the amount on what the property is worth now, after any existing mortgage, not what it will be worth once the work is complete. Check how much headroom there is before you commission a big project.
Staged payments
For larger projects some lenders release money in stages as work is certified, which follows how contractors bill. Not all do this, so say at the outset if the project is phased.
What lenders check

A valuation, the title and any existing charges, contractor quotes, planning or building regulation consents and the company’s accounts. A schedule of works with costs and dates shows that the project is under control.
considerations: You are borrowing against the building
If repayments are missed, the lender can act against the property, which may be where the business trades from. Be sure the company can afford the loan if trading dips during the works.
Planning and consents come first
Delays in permissions or building regulations approval can hold up the money and the builders. Start those processes early and tell the broker where each stands.
Value added is not guaranteed
A refurbishment may not raise the property’s value by as much as it cost. Judge it by what it does for the business, such as saving running costs or enabling more income, not by resale value alone.
faqs: Can I borrow against my premises to refurbish them?

Yes, if the company owns the building, or a director or another company does and agrees to offer it as security. The lender will value the property, check existing borrowing against it and look at the plans and costs. A broker can say which lenders are likely to be interested.
How much can I borrow?

It depends on the property’s value, any existing mortgage, the company’s accounts and the cost of the work. Lenders generally lend a share of the value, so there is a limit. A broker can estimate what is realistic once they know the property and the plan.
Do I need planning permission first?

For structural changes or a change of use, usually yes, and lenders often expect permissions and approvals to be in place or applied for. Cosmetic work generally does not need it. Check with your local authority, and tell the broker where the process stands.
Can the loan be paid out in stages?

Some lenders offer this for larger projects, releasing money as work is completed and certified. It lowers interest on money not yet used. Not all lenders do it, so ask the broker to look for it if your project runs over several months.
What if the work costs more than the quote?

Overruns are common, especially in older buildings. Build a contingency into the amount you borrow and keep some cash in reserve. Increasing a secured loan midway can mean new valuations and legal work, so getting the figure right at the start saves time and cost.

secured-business-loans|working-capital.h1: Secured business loans for working capital
secured-business-loans|working-capital.title: Secured Business Loans for Working Capital | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|working-capital.desc: When a UK limited company might use a secured loan for working capital, such as releasing equity or replacing short-term debts, and what to weigh first.
secured-business-loans|working-capital.lead: Releasing equity or replacing short-term debts can lower monthly outgoings, at the price of putting an asset behind everyday cash needs.
intro: Using a secured loan for working capital means putting a building or other asset behind money that will be spent on wages, suppliers and rent. It is not the usual choice, because day-to-day needs rise and fall while a secured loan is a long, fixed commitment. It makes sense in a narrower set of cases: the company owns property that is not working hard, it carries several short-term debts with heavy instalments, or it has outgrown what unsecured lenders will provide. A longer term can turn heavy monthly repayments into manageable ones.

For example, a building contractor with £3m in annual revenue might owe £150,000 across a merchant cash advance, two short loans and a tax arrangement, all repaid weekly or monthly. Borrowing £200,000 over ten years against its yard could clear those and leave a lower monthly outgoing and some cash in hand. Lenders will want to know why the cash is needed and how the business avoids needing it again, because borrowing long term for a short-term problem only moves the problem further down the road.
uses: Replacing several short-term debts
Combine merchant advances, short loans and overdraft use into one longer, lower repayment.
Releasing equity for a cash buffer
Raise money against property the company owns, to build a reserve for slower months.
Stabilising after a hard year
Rebuild working capital following a loss-making period, where trading has recovered but reserves have not.
Supporting a big contract
Carry the costs of a large order that will take many months to be paid, where invoice finance or an overdraft would be too small.
fit: Matching a long term to a short need

Because the term is long, instalments are small, but you pay interest for years on money that may be spent within months. Some lenders allow early repayment, so check the terms and consider paying it down when cash allows.
Amounts and security

Secured working capital loans typically start in the low six figures and depend on the equity available. Lenders subtract existing borrowing from the property’s value, then lend a share of what is left.
What lenders look at

They want to understand why working capital is short, so expect questions about margins, how long customers take to pay, the order book and any losses. Management accounts and a cash flow forecast help show recovery is under way.
considerations: Property at risk for running costs
If the business struggles again, the lender can act against the building that secures the loan. Think about whether a smaller, unsecured or revolving facility could do the job with less at risk.
Flexible facilities often fit better
A revolving credit facility, an overdraft or invoice finance moves with your cash needs and can cost less when balances are small. A broker may suggest one alongside or instead of a secured loan.
Costs and early repayment
Valuation, legal and arrangement fees and any early repayment charge can make a secured loan expensive to take out and expensive to leave. Ask for the full list before deciding.
faqs: Can I use a secured loan for working capital?

Yes, many lenders allow it, provided the company has security to offer and can afford the repayments. It is a bigger commitment than a short loan or overdraft, so a broker will usually ask why it is needed and may suggest other facilities that put less at risk.
Is it cheaper than unsecured working capital?

Sometimes, because the security lowers the lender’s risk, and a long term reduces each instalment. But fees and the length of the loan can raise the total cost. Compare the total repayable, not only the monthly figure, and ask a broker to show both routes.
Can I repay it early when cash improves?

Many lenders allow early repayment, but some charge a fee or require interest for a minimum period. If you expect to clear the loan in a year or two, check the terms before you sign, since this could be the difference between a good and a poor choice.
Will it help if I have arrears elsewhere?

A secured loan can be used to clear arrears and other debts, and some lenders will consider it. They will look closely at why the arrears arose and whether trading has recovered. A broker can tell you how lenders may view your history before you apply.
What security do lenders accept?

Mainly property, including the company’s premises or a director’s property, and sometimes a debenture over company assets. The value of the security, after existing charges, sets how much you can borrow. A broker can explain which type each lender prefers.

secured-business-loans|buying-stock.h1: Secured business loans for buying stock
secured-business-loans|buying-stock.title: Secured Business Loans for Buying Stock | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|buying-stock.desc: When a UK limited company buying stock in large volumes might use a secured loan, and why a revolving facility often suits repeat purchases better.
secured-business-loans|buying-stock.lead: For one large stock purchase that outgrows short-term facilities, a loan secured on property or company assets over a longer term.
intro: Most stock is bought with short-term finance, so a secured loan is a choice for particular situations: a wholesaler buying several container loads at once, a manufacturer stockpiling raw materials ahead of a price rise or a builders’ merchant stocking a new branch. Amounts of this size can go beyond what the company’s trading figures support alone, and the loan may need to run longer than a seasonal facility would. A lender who takes security over property, or a debenture covering the company’s assets including its stock, can offer more than an unsecured lender, usually with a longer repayment period.

The risk is that stock sells quickly and the loan runs for years. For example, an importer of kitchenware with £4m in annual revenue might borrow £300,000 over five years against its warehouse to pay for the stock of a new range before it is sold, repaying from the margin on the sales. If the range sells in six months, the company still has years of repayments, so it needs to be confident that the purchase is not a one-off need that a shorter facility would cover.
uses: Importing in bulk
Pay overseas suppliers for full container loads, where minimum order sizes and shipping costs favour larger, less frequent orders.
Stocking a new branch or warehouse
Fill a new site with the range it needs before it opens, when the cost lands months before income.
Buying raw materials ahead of price rises
Lock in metal, timber or components at today’s price for production over the coming year.
Slow-moving or maturing stock
Carry goods that are slow to sell or need time to mature, such as specialist machinery, wine or furniture ranges.
fit: Amounts and terms

Secured stock loans usually start from the low six figures and run over several years. A term of three to seven years is common, although stock that sells in months argues for the shorter end, or for a different facility altogether.
Property or debenture security

The lender may take a charge on property, a debenture covering stock and other assets, or both. Stock alone is rarely enough, since it can be hard to value and quick to change. A broker can explain how each lender treats it.
What lenders check
Stock turn and ageing, gross margins, supplier and customer terms and the accounts. A schedule of stock, with ages and values, helps show what is being financed and how fast it should sell.
considerations: A long loan for goods that sell quickly
Match the loan to the pace of sales. If the stock turns in a few months, paying for five years is poor value, and a revolving credit facility or trade finance may fit the cycle better.
Stock can lose value
Fashion, technology and perishable goods can fall in price, leaving the loan worth more than the stock. The property pledged as security then carries the gap.
Concentration risk
A large buy tied to one supplier, one product or one currency raises the stakes. Changes in exchange rates or delays in shipping can strain cash flow while repayments continue.
faqs: Why use a secured loan to buy stock?

Usually because the amount is large or the company wants a longer term than short-term stock facilities give. The security allows larger sums, and the longer term spreads the cost. The trade-off is that property or other assets are at risk, so it suits only specific purchases.
Can the stock be the security?

A debenture can give the lender a charge over the company’s assets, including stock, but lenders often want property as well because stock is harder to value and can change quickly. A broker can explain how each lender treats stock and what else they might require.
Is a revolving facility better for stock?

Often, if you buy repeatedly through the year, because you draw what you need and repay when stock sells, paying interest only on what is used. A secured loan suits a single large purchase. A broker can look at both and show you how each would work for your cycle.
What about importing and currency?

If you pay suppliers in another currency, exchange rate moves can change what you owe in pounds, and payment terms such as letters of credit may apply. Ask the broker whether trade finance fits better, and discuss currency risk with your bank or accountant.
How long does it take to arrange?

Longer than unsecured borrowing, because of the valuation and legal work on the security. If you have a shipping date or a supplier’s price deadline, tell the broker at the start so they can plan the timetable around it and flag any risk.
